scenes.title: The Hypothetical Halting Tester
scenes.visual: A large rectangular box labeled 'H(P, i)' appears in the center. An arrow labeled 'Program P & Input i' enters from the left. Two arrows exit to the right: one labeled 'Halts' pointing to a green text 'TRUE', and another labeled 'Loops Forever' pointing to a red text 'FALSE'.
scenes.narration: Imagine we could build a universal program, H, that takes any program P and its input i, and correctly predicts if it will eventually halt or loop forever.

scenes.title: Constructing the Paradoxical Machine
scenes.visual: A new outer rectangle labeled 'Machine D(P)' is drawn around a modified copy of H. An arrow labeled 'Program P' enters D. Inside D, P is duplicated into two inputs entering H(P, P). The output 'Halts' from H leads to an infinite loop visual (a spinning circle with an arrow). The output 'Loops Forever' leads to a simple 'Stop' text box.
scenes.narration: Now we construct a new program, D, which feeds its input program P to H as both the program and its input. If H says P halts, D deliberately enters an infinite loop; if H says P loops, D immediately halts.

scenes.title: The Self-Referential Contradiction
scenes.visual: The input label for Machine D changes to 'D itself', making the full diagram represent D(D). A large yellow question mark appears over the center. Red highlighting flashes between the two contradictory paths: 'If H says Halts -> D loops' vs 'If H says Loops -> D halts'. Finally, a big red 'X' drawn over the box H.
scenes.narration: What happens when we run D on itself? If H predicts D halts, D loops forever. If H predicts D loops, D halts. Because both outcomes create an impossible contradiction, such a program H can never exist.
